To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

hydraulic redistribution was observed in a mallee eukalypt species, Eucalypt us kochii sub sp borealis, with high rates occurring in landscape positions with access to fresh groundwater, and that the net volume of water moved from deep soil by hydraulic redistribution was calculated to be equivalent to up to 27 % of transpiration.
Eucalypt trees can access groundwater at depth, and can move water from the deeper soil to the upper soil layers.
hydraulic redistribution is an important mechanism by which Eucalypt kochii sub. borealis trees access water in the Western Australian Wheatbelt.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of hydraulic redistribution in water use and salinity management of a mallee eukalypt in a variable water environment.
the role of deep rooted trees in reducing the salinisation potential of cleared land.
understanding how the hydrological and hydraulic properties of a landscape can affect the water relations of trees.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the water use patterns of E. kochii sub. sp borealis are complex and influenced by the landscape position and the depth of groundwater.

hydraulic redistribution in this species was a significant component of the water balance and that the magnitude of this effect was dependent on water availability and the soil water potential gradient.
the net effect of hydraulic redistribution on water use by E. kochii sub sp. borealis is uncertain, but may be significant in some situations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hydraulic redistribution may be an important mechanism by which trees access deep soil water, particularly in landscapes that have abundant groundwater.
hydraulic redistribution can occur in a wide range of landscape positions with different soil water availability.
the hydraulic redistribution by E. kochii sub sp. borealis in a saline environment was significant but not large enough to have any effect on the salinisation processes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hydraulic redistribution can be a significant component of water use by plants with deep roots in water-limited landscapes.
hydraulic redistribution is a significant process in Eucalypts and may be a useful tool for managing water use in the Western Australian Wheatbelt.

E. kochii sub sp borealis can access deep groundwater in a range of landscape positions, and can redistribute water laterally from deep to shallow soil horizons, but the net effect on transpiration may be negligible.
